summary:
When a disaster hits, the sky is usually full of cloud and smoke, which is exactly when optical satellites go blind. NISAR’s radar sees through all of it, day or night. The catch is that radar data is hard to read unless you’re an expert, and any single signal can fool you. So I built Pas de Trois, an interactive globe that reads three NISAR signals together: phase, coherence and backscatter.

Pick an event and the globe tracks NISAR’s live orbit and tells you whether it actually saw the place. Radar Lens shows the imagery. Dancing Fringes turns phase into visible rings of ground movement. Change Fingerprint compares all three signals to work out what kind of change happened, like shifting ground, damage or flooding. Then Is This Normal? checks the result against how much that spot usually varies, so everyday noise isn’t mistaken for real change.

It matters because responders, journalists and students shouldn’t need a radar PhD to ask what changed here. A responder can see where to look first, a reporter can check a claim, and a student can learn how radar works by playing with real data. When the evidence is too weak, it says so instead of showing a confident map that might be wrong. No single signal tells the whole story, but together the three can.
details:
The problem. When disaster strikes, the sky usually goes dark first: smoke, ash, storm cloud, night. That’s exactly when optical satellites go blind. NISAR, the new NASA-ISRO radar mission, sees straight through all of it. But radar data is notoriously hard to read, and any single radar signal can lie to you. A flooded field and a freshly plowed one can look the same. I wanted to build something that lets anyone, not just radar scientists, look at a disaster through NISAR’s eyes and get an honest answer.

What it does. Pas de Trois reads three NISAR signals together instead of one. Phase reveals whether the ground moved. Coherence reveals whether the surface was disturbed. Backscatter reveals whether it got rougher or wetter. On their own, each is ambiguous. Together, they form a fingerprint. On a 3D globe, you pick an event like the Krakatau eruption and walk through five steps. First, see NISAR’s live orbit and whether it actually passed over. Then view the radar image. Next, watch ground movement appear as rings of interference fringes. Then let the three signals classify the change as movement, damage or flooding. Finally, check it against how much that exact spot normally varies.

Why it matters. The last step is the one I care about most. Every answer comes with a confidence score, and when the evidence is too weak, Pas de Trois says so instead of drawing a dramatic map that might be wrong. A responder learns where to look first. A journalist can test a claim before publishing it. A student can learn what radar actually measures. And because NISAR maps the planet every 12 days, the answers can keep up with events.

How it’s built. It runs as a CesiumJS globe in Vue 3, deployed on Vercel. A Python pipeline pulls NISAR’s radar images (GCOV) and ground-motion maps (GUNW) from NASA Earthdata and the Alaska Satellite Facility, using asf_search, earthaccess, h5py, NumPy, rasterio and SciPy. NASA GIBS supplies global imagery, USGS feeds supply live hazards, and public orbit data drives the satellite track.

What makes it different. Most radar tools hand you one layer and assume you’re an expert. Pas de Trois treats radar like a dance for three, where the meaning comes from how the signals move together. It also treats uncertainty as a feature, not something to hide.
